items.title: Endless pile of Needle In Haystack games begins to emerge, as viral hit imitator's devs claim their code was nicked by a genAI-using clone
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: In a metaphor far too on the nose to turn into any form of fiction, at least without the writer getting mercilessly cyberbullied, a game about finding a needle
items.text:
In a metaphor far too on the nose to turn into any form of fiction, at least without the writer getting mercilessly cyberbullied, a game about finding a needle in a haystack has now become the genuine needle at the heart of a pile of imitators. A pile so large, in fact, one copycat game stands accused of ripping code from another.

NoGlyph, developers of Needle In A Haystack, have claimed that their code's been nicked by A Game About Needle In A Haystack devs Little Field Studios. The former game was released on September 29th this year. The latter came out on October 16th. Both offer players a chance to go hunting for metal implements in piles of horse food, and both appear to have been inspired by the as-yet unreleased Needle In A Haystack Simulator, which gained notoriety after serving as the basis of a viral tweet in August.

These are just three of the needle-in-haystack games which've massed on Steam since that clip got a bunch of eyeballs, as various people look to fill the world's apparent desire to hunt stiching implements on a farm.

"Yesterday, on October 16th a game called 'A Game About Needle In A Haystack' by Little Field Studios came out on Steam," a Needle In A Haystack dev called Jahvin wrote in a Steam post over the weekend. "It contains code copied from our game. To be clear, this is about our actual code, not a similar idea or similar mechanics.

"The haystack in our game, meaning how it's drawn, how you dig into it and how gold, lapis and diamond hay work, is something that took a long time to get working properly. When we looked through their game's files, we found 13 of our classes inside it with the exact same names. More than half of the functions in that part match ours exactly. Some of our own error messages are still in there word for word, including one that points to a shader from our project that doesn't exist in their game.

"The copied code matches the versions of our free demo we put out on September 20 and 21, a few weeks before their release. From what we can tell, the rest of their game (the art, the sounds, the other systems) is their own work. Our problem is the hay code."

So, not an apparent copycat calling out another apparent copycat solely for its premise, but an accusation that things have evolved to the point of a studio directly ripping specific code and assets. The Needle In A Haystack devs added that they've filed a copyright notice with Valve and saved off a copy of their findings as proof.

A Game About Needle In A Haystack, the accused, boasts a genAI disclosure in its Steam description, but this only makes clear that the tech was used to produce the game's logo. If the hay code situation is as Jahvin described, that could suggest the potential for AI-assisted decompilation to have been at play in the alleged copying, but there doesn't seem to be any definite confirmation of that as of writing.

Dev concerns about AI being used to easily replicate games have been on the rise, following the recent boom in genAI-assisted decompilation. Just last week, the makers of a game called Drunken Goddess Reflux announced they'd cancelled plans for a public demo in favour of limited-access playtesting sessions, citing concern that "the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools, and that such works could be released before our launch".

Honestly, I'm just terrified that the ever-growing mound of needle-in-haystack variants will eventually grow to the point of causing Steam's vast barn of games to burst, sending horse-shaped westerns, pitchfork-shaped fantasy RPGs, and water trough-shaped games aimed at thirsty horndogs flying across the plains of the net.

items.title: Metal band Genitorturers claims a Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines remake is coming, getting a dozen crusty nerds way too worked up
items.author: ted.litchfield@futurenet.com (Ted Litchfield)
items.summary: Original Story: This one is thin, man, but it has to do with one of my favorite games of all time, while the circumstances of the rumor are just kind of neat
items.text:
Original Story: This one is thin, man, but it has to do with one of my favorite games of all time, while the circumstances of the rumor are just kind of neat and weird, even if it turns out to be nothing. User Few_Interview8222 on the Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines subreddit reported back from a Genitorturers show in Brooklyn, New York. Partway through the set, the band supposedly told the crowd that a VtMB remake is happening.

Genitorturers played at Brooklyn's The Meadows as part of their "Live + Lewd Tour" on October 15. We've reached out to both rights-holder Activision (one of several, it's complicated) and Genitorturers' representation, and will update this story if we hear back.

Why would an industrial metal band started in Orlando in 1986 have this information?

In addition to a killer score by Rik Schaffer, Bloodlines featured wonderfully era-appropriate licensed tracks from metal bands⁠—they were mostly used as diegetic music in the nightclubs and bars of Los Angeles. The Genitorturers track Lecher Bitch was the pitch-perfect theme of The Last Round, a downtown LA dive bar frequented by the Anarch faction of vampires.

What if they're wrong?

Multiple commenters on the Reddit thread point out that this could have been a confused, untimely, misinterpreted, or all of the above reference to last year's Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines 2. It's the sort of almost-but-not-quite thing you might expect from an artist with tangential awareness of a secondary fanbase they picked up over the years.

A VtMB remake is also the sort of project you could see getting pingponged around between various actors and stakeholders: started, stopped, shopped around, etc. It'd be a situation ripe for collaborators on the periphery acting on outdated information.

What if they're right?

Rad! I think? It'd depend on who's doing it. More and more, I'm beginning to distrust anyone not named "Nightdive" when it comes to commercial remasters. See also: The recent Shogun 2 debacle and the fate of Deus Ex Remastered.

Bloodlines is such a wild, janky, PC gaming package that Nightdive is the only studio I'd trust to not only do a remaster right, but also to bring on legendary modder Werner "Wesp5" Spahl, the man who's been keeping Bloodlines alive with one of the most impactful unofficial patch projects in gaming. A more ground-up remake would offer equally daunting challenges, like matching the one-of-a-kind mood and look Troika managed to evoke.

Why should you care?

Bloodlines is one of my very favorite games and an incredible RPG that's well worth your time. To the uninitiated, I like to pitch it as an evolutionary missing link between 2D Fallout and New Vegas. Bloodlines boasts the open-ended design and reactivity of Fallout in 3D for the very first time (Bloodlines leads Leonard Boyarsky and Jason Anderson were senior talent on Fallout 1).

Unlike New Vegas' wide open world, however, Bloodlines had a more linear, but still loose sequence of zones on a world map to explore. Bloodlines' Y2K, gothic, noir interpretation of Los Angeles is one of the coolest worlds ever presented in an RPG.

A Nightdive treatment would be my preferred outcome: build on Wesp5's work and compensate him accordingly, then make it more accessible on more platforms at a modest markup over the original game. Bloodlines 1 can be had for $20 on Steam and GOG, but it's practically always on sale.

Even if it turns out to be nothing, this is still just a neat, newsworthy little incident to behold—Genitorturers shouting out an obscure, beloved RPG like this 22 years later, and maybe getting a couple genre nerds like me a little too excited on the way.

items.text:
PlayStation Officially Delists Major First-Party Games

Custom Image by Casandra Ronning

Published Oct 20, 2026, 6:02 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

Sometimes it truly does feel like we're entering the darkest timeline for video games. From mass layoffs, huge hardware price hikes and more Triple-A flops than hits on our hands, it is not really a great time to be a fan of small-screen escapism. Add to that, PlayStation's relentless, misjudged quest to outlaw physical media, and it feels like a war is brewing between gamers and the gaming industry. Sadly, there's more bad news hitting us gamers. Let's get into it.

The PS store (specifically in North America) has started to delist some of our favorite games. With the future of physical media on the PlayStation platform very much coming to an end, this may make getting your hands on some beloved classics extremely difficult. As reported by TheGamer, Knack 2, God of War 3 Remastered and Uncharted: The Nathan Drake Collection have all disappeared from the PS store in select parts of the world.

While it's unlikely anyone is pining for Knack 2, both God of War 3 Remastered and Uncharted: The Nathan Drake Collection are absolute classics. These games could be considered the pillars that the previous PlayStation generation built its success on, and it boggles the mind that they would remove them from the store. If you already own (a touchy point these days) digital copies of these games, you will still have access to download and play them from your library, but any newcomers won't be able to purchase them.

Flash forward to next year, and if PlayStation goes through with their promise of no more physical discs being produced, then player choice is starting to feel like it's out of our hands. It's not all doom and gloom though, as updated reports show that the games have only been temporarily removed due to pricing errors across other regions. But the cynic in me believes the God of War 3 remaster was removed in order to pump more sales towards the upcoming God of War Trilogy Remake for PS5.

items.author: Clint Worthington

items.text:
Of the universe of Taylor Sheridan AARP-for-aging-’80s-guys dramas aimed squarely at the silent majority, “Tulsa King” is by far the most charming. Flitting somewhere between “Yellowstone” and “Get Shorty” in its tale of a New York goombah (Sylvester Stallone) starting his criminal enterprise all over again in Oklahoma, the show has spent three seasons simply letting its bulging cast of characters engage in soap-opera theatrics, squaring off against rival gang members and, in this last set of episodes, a vindictive bourbon distiller played by Robert Patrick. (Spoiler alert: Sly burns him at the stake in the season finale. I guess it’s the only way to be sure with the T-1000.) But in season four, “Tulsa King” finally feels like it’s getting lost in the literal and metaphorical sauce.

After taking over Patrick’s distillery, Dwight “The General” Manfredi (Stallone) is finally ready to legitimize his enterprises (well, some of them) and settle down with his girlfriend of three seasons, Margaret Devereaux (Dana Delany). Unfortunately, mysterious circumstances arise at the end of the season premiere that leave Dwight in deep mourning and unsure where his businesses stand with the government. That latter concern is compounded by the elevation of lieutenant governor Amanda Clark (Gretchen Mol), a by-the-books do-gooder who knows Dwight’s game and wants to shut him down permanently, to the top office.

That’s not Dwight’s only concern, of course; his old mafia family in New York City keeps gunning for the profits he’s been building in the Southwest, especially now that his old nemesis, Quiet Ray (James Russo), is fully in charge. What’s more, a greedy German AI tech bro (Flula Borg) is threatening to take Margaret’s horse ranch by eminent domain to turn the land into a data center.

(L-R): Scarlet Stallone as Spencer, Martin Starr as Bodhi, and Jay Will as Tyson in Tulsa King, episode 1, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

All these conflicts and more stud “Tulsa King”‘s new season, and that’s not even getting into Bodhi’s (Martin Starr) flirtation with wine forgery, or Tyson’s (Jay Will) burgeoning rap career. And let’s not forget Dwight’s unsteady alliance with government spook Musso (Kevin Pollak) from last season and how that dovetails with Dwight’s existing animus with fellow capo Bevilaqua (Frank Grillo). Hey, there are a lot of aging character actors to pay; we gotta give them something to do, right? We should be thankful Samuel L. Jackson isn’t here to soak up more screen time, as he’s supposedly off building his own spinoff down in New Orleans.

“Tulsa King,” at this point, is more overstuffed than a turducken, with a cast so bloated that the gang is juggling at least three or four different schemes at once. Even Sly is getting a little tired; sure, some of that is Dwight’s puffed-up grief, but some of it is the older actor slowing down. (The show even writes a cane into Dwight’s ensemble; it’s passed off as an occasional knee injury that flares up from time to time, but I get the feeling that cane’s here to stay.) Even Sly coasting is compelling enough to watch, but you can tell the rest of the cast has to shore up their game to help carry this thing. This is especially true of Annabella Sciorra’s Joanne, Dwight’s enterprising sister and partner in crime, who slowly becomes the show’s heart and soul.

Gretchen Mol as Amanda Clark in Tulsa King, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

In fact, you get the most enjoyment from showrunner Dave Erickson and his writing team’s occasional lapses into the ridiculous. Italian enforcer pals Goodie (Chris Caldovino) and Vince (Vincent Piazza) shoot their way out of a white supremacist meeting at a restaurant they happen to be eating at; “You just got robbed by two swarthy Mediterraneans!” they shout as they leave. Dwight mournfully asks an AI chatbot whether God exists, and the scene is treated as if it’s dispensing therapeutic wisdom from on high. Someone gets their head crushed in the jaws of a fossilized dinosaur skull. In these scenes, “Tulsa King” ekes out a kind of campy enjoyment. It’s just a shame you have to sift through so many diluted storylines to get there. (The less said about the budding romance between Garrett Hedlund’s Mitch and Scarlet Stallone’s Spencer, the better.)

It’d be dishonest to claim “Tulsa King” doesn’t offer consistent diversion, even amid the myriad components of Dwight’s business empire and all the spinning plates therein. But this season’s villains don’t compel (including everyone’s favorite “My Son Hunter” director Robert Davi as a creaky enforcer who looks like he can barely stand, let alone take out fools), and so many of the plot threads feel like filler to give Dwight’s bloated entourage things to do. The bulk of the show’s charm falls squarely on Stallone’s broad shoulders, and even he’s starting to lose a step. Here’s hoping the show can get its affairs in order in an already-announced season five, or this vital leg of the Taylor Sheridan universe will go, well, the way of the dinosaur.

Full season screened for review. Premieres October 16th on Paramount+.

Writing from the Chicagoland area in Illinois, Robert is an avid movie watcher and will take just about any excuse to find time to go to his local movie theaters. Robert graduated from Bradley University with degrees in Journalism and Game Design with a minor in Film Studies. Robert tries his best to keep up with all the latest movie releases, from those released in theaters to those released on streaming. While he doesn't always keep up with the latest TV shows, he makes it a goal to watch nearly every major new release possible. He has been honing his craft and following any and all movie news all his life, leading up to now, where he has a vast knowledge of film and film history. He also logs every movie that he watches on his Letterboxd page, and has hosted a weekly online movie night with his closest friends for over 6 years.

For as long as cinema has been a mainstay in culture and society, comedy movies have been the perfect avenue for film to bring joy and laughter to audiences worldwide. Some of the most recognized and well-known movies of all time are comedy films, with every filmmaking era having its standout picks of amazing comedies that define the era. The 2020s have already proven to be another great decade for comedy, with many hilarious and iconic films already released.

The number of iconic, widely renowned comedy movies released in the 2020s is a great sign that even more inventive comedies will be released in the rest of the decade. Especially with the rise of streaming services, the amount of high-quality comedies being released is at a staggeringly high rate. From massive blockbuster successes that millions worldwide have watched to more niche indie darlings that received massive critical praise and awards nominations, there is no shortage of notable comedies released in the 2020s.

25
'No Hard Feelings' (2023)

Image via Sony Pictures

The raunchy R-rated studio comedy is a specific style of film that, while massively popular throughout the 2000s and 2010s, has seemingly fallen out of favor in the modern landscape of franchises and streaming services. However, one major example that proved the genre's fluidity and proven success is No Hard Feelings, which harkens back to the classic type of chaotic, sex-fueled comedies in the vein of Superbad and Saving Sarah Marshall. The film stars Jennifer Lawrence as Maddie, a girl who, in an attempt to earn money to save her childhood home, agrees to be paid by a 19-year-old's helicopter parents to go on a date with him before college.

There is an inherent charm and honesty present within No Hard Feelings that is largely missing from comedies of the modern era, making its simple execution and style hit that much harder for a contemporary audience. Lawrence proves that she has exceptional comedic chops in the film, largely elevating the material and committing to the chaos required to make its premise work well. Especially for those who are looking for a comedy in the same vein as classics from previous eras, No Hard Feelings is definitely worth seeking out.

24
'Between the Temples' (2024)

Image via Sony Pictures Classics

There's an inherently difficult balancing act when it comes to making a great cringe-comedy film, as their goal of finding laughter out of the most uncomfortable of situations is tricky to pull off effectively. Easily one of the best modern films that flourishes in this distinct style of painfully awkward comedy is Between the Temples, which acts as a masterclass of awkward personality in all regards. The film follows a grief-stricken cantor forging an unexpected friendship with his grade school music teacher, who has reentered his life as his new adult Bat Mitzvah student.

Between the Temples makes the most out of its quirky and irregular characters, placing them in increasingly uncomfortable and painful situations where the only reaction is to laugh out of pain. It's certainly a comedic style that doesn't align with everyone, yet when it's working at the height of its powers, it makes for one of the funniest experiences imaginable. The film's energy feels in line with the classic rom-com works of Elaine May, especially sharing a lot of energy with films like The Heartbreak Kid.

23
'Another Round' (2020)

Another Round is a Danish film that follows a group of four high school teachers who, as a way to add some spice and variety into their increasingly boring lives, launch their own experiment in making day-to-day life more enjoyable. They attempt to continuously drink alcoholic drinks to hold a constant low level of intoxication going forward, including while working their job as well as their time at home. The experiment proves itself to come with upsides as well as major difficulties, as it becomes a balancing act for each of them to adjust to the new lifestyle.

While international movies always seem to be harder sells for more general audiences, Another Round is easily one of the most accessible and adaptable international films to be released in recent memory. The film's very simple yet highly effective premise leads to a great deal of comedy and shenanigans, which are only further amplified by the terrific performances of everyone involved and the great directing style of Thomas Veinterberg. The film made enough of a splash worldwide that there are even plans for an English remake starring Leonardo DiCaprio.

22
'Emma.' (2020)

Image via Focus Features

Adapted from the iconic classic Jane Austen novel, Emma follows the story of the well-meaning but selfish young woman of Emma, living in 1800s England as she meddles with the love lives of her friends and family. As she continues to play matchmaker in the lives of everyone around her, Emma soon enough finds herself unknowingly at the center of her own romance as it begins to unfold around her.

The story of Emma has been adapted to film a multitude of times throughout film history, both through direct adaptations of the novel and loose adaptations like the teen sensation Clueless. However, Autumn de Wilde's Emma is able to perfectly combine the themes and attributes of the original novel with enough modern flair and conventions to make it an exceptional comedic period piece. The true highlight of the film is Anya Taylor-Joy, who provides an iconic and scene-stealing comedic performance in the leading role of Emma.

21
'Theater Camp' (2023)

Image Via Searchlight

A love letter to the small-scale, chaotic nature of summer camp and amateur theater, Theater Camp is equal parts defined by its endless charm as it is by its embracing of its nonsensical supporting cast. The mockumentary follows a scrappy upstate New York theater falling into shambles after its beloved founder ends up in a coma, forcing the eccentric staff and the founder's failure of a son to keep the camp afloat for the summer.

No other film has such an intelligent, fundamental understanding of the ins and outs of youth theater quite like Theater Camp, making for the perfect setup to absolutely make fun of it with pitch-perfect satire. Each member of the supporting cast gets time to shine, whether it be the charmingly idiotic Troy (Jimmy Tatro) or the inseparable pair of Amos (Ben Platt) and Rebecca-Diane (Molly Gordon). While the film was originally overlooked during its theatrical release due to releasing at the same time as Barbie and Oppenheimer, it soon found a new life and fan-favorite status on streaming.

20
'Hit Man' (2024)

Image via Netflix

Richard Linklater has helmed a wide variety of exceptional comedy films over the years, including the likes of School of Rock and Dazed and Confused. Hit Man is simply the latest smash hit comedy from the director, using an ingenious premise to get a wide variety of laughs and mileage out of one of Hollywood's biggest rising stars, Glen Powell. The film sees Powell as Gary Johnson, a mild-mannered professor who works on the side as a fake hitman in police stings, who finds himself in the middle of a major predicament when he begins to fall for his latest client.

Hit Man fully delivers on the comedic potential of its concept, giving free rein for Powell to show off his comedic chops in a wide variety of fun and hilarious performance styles and personalities. However, what continues to make the film one of the biggest and most acclaimed comedies of the streaming service era is the signature heart and charm that is present within all of Linklater's works. The phone call sequence at the end is especially one of the greatest comedic setups in recent memory, and is emblematic of the entire film's overwhelming charm and electrifying energy.

19
'Palm Springs' (2020)

Image via NEON

Palm Springs follows the story of carefree spirit Nyles and reluctant Maid of honor Sarah, who, after their brief encounter during a Palm Springs wedding, find themselves at the center of a supernatural event. The duo is stuck in an endless time loop where they are forced to repeat the day of the wedding over and over and subsequently exhaust all possibilities of what could happen on the wedding day. With endless time on their hands, the duo soon form a connection and bond, which begins to crack as the duo attempts to find a way to escape.

Time-loop movies have become a staple of comedy ever since the massively popular Groundhog Day, yet Palm Springs stands out as the first comedy since Groundhog Day to make perfect comedic use of the premise. Palm Springs understands both the inherent comedy and potential present within time loops, as well as the eventual dread and horror that come as a result of exhausted possibilities. The primary focus of the film being on a duo as opposed to a singular person only further adds to the comedic potential, as well as the inevitable crash and burn.

18
'The Drama' (2026)

Image via A24

Quickly making a name for itself as one of the defining dark comedies of the decade, Kristoffer Borgli's The Drama isn't afraid to delve into some fundamentally uncomfortable subject matter while simultaneously finding the comedic elements within such unsettling concepts. The film sees happily engaged Emma (Zendaya) and Charlie (Robert Pattinson) have their bonds tested after some shocking truths from Emma's past come to life in what was supposed to be a fun game of awkward truths.

The Drama gets a lot of mileage out of pushing the strange absurdities of its painful central concept, one that can't truly be stated without spoiling the movie but undeniably is considered a major taboo to discuss in the realm of comedy. However, it's tackled with such inherent precision and finesse, focusing more on the psychological dynamics of these characters instead of the pain of the concept itself, that it allows the film to greatly succeed as one of the funniest yet darkest films of 2026.

17
'The Worst Person in the World' (2021)

Image via SF Studios

A strikingly prolific and brilliant coming-of-age story about the transitionary period of young adulthood, The Worst Person in the World is a singular cinematic experience that feels timeless in its execution. The film chronicles four years in the life of Julie (Renate Reinsve) as she navigates a troubled love life and struggles to find her career path. The chaos and unpredictability of her life lead her to look inward in hopes of discovering who she truly is as a person.

The Worst Person in the World provides a more intimate look at a period of time not often explored for its development and growth, yet is undeniably important and emblematic of modern human experience. The film blends its serious and impactful messaging with an array of comedic, lighthearted moments, with deeply engrossing characters to further amplify the themes and energy of the film. Even for those who don't normally watch international filmmaking, this Norwegian film is absolutely worth watching for any fans of serious dramatic rom-coms.

Image via Searchlight Pictures

The Menu follows the story of a couple who travel off to a coastal island in order to eat at a highly prestigious, exclusive restaurant in which the head chef, Slowik, has prepared an extensive and lavish menu. As the night progresses, it becomes more and more apparent that the planned menu and dinner are much more sinister, as the guests' lives are on the line. Already an outsider to this exclusive and high-class world, Margot attempts to do everything that she can to escape the dinner before it's too late.

The Menu is a film that is as sinister and disturbing as it is hilarious and satirical in its lambasting and portrayal of the upper class and the culture that it perpetuates. The film is filled with hilarious characters and set pieces that complement the rising tension and stakes of the film perfectly. The film is all brought together by the comedically terrifying central performance of Ralph Fiennes as Chef Slowik, who perfectly balances being a cold and calculating villainous force with the comedic service industry revenge fantasy.

Especially for those who are looking for a comedy in the same vein as classics from previous eras, No Hard Feelings is definitely worth seeking out.

24
'Between the Temples' (2024)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/5-8.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Jason Schwartzman and Carol Kane sit on a couch in Between the Temples.

blocks.x: Image via Sony Pictures Classics

There's an inherently difficult balancing act when it comes to making a great cringe-comedy film, as their goal of finding laughter out of the most uncomfortable of situations is tricky to pull off effectively. Easily one of the best modern films that flourishes in this distinct style of painfully awkward comedy is Between the Temples, which acts as a masterclass of awkward personality in all regards. The film follows a grief-stricken cantor forging an unexpected friendship with his grade school music teacher, who has reentered his life as his new adult Bat Mitzvah student.

Between the Temples makes the most out of its quirky and irregular characters, placing them in increasingly uncomfortable and painful situations where the only reaction is to laugh out of pain. It's certainly a comedic style that doesn't align with everyone, yet when it's working at the height of its powers, it makes for one of the funniest experiences imaginable. The film's energy feels in line with the classic rom-com works of Elaine May, especially sharing a lot of energy with films like The Heartbreak Kid.

23
'Another Round' (2020)

Another Round is a Danish film that follows a group of four high school teachers who, as a way to add some spice and variety into their increasingly boring lives, launch their own experiment in making day-to-day life more enjoyable. They attempt to continuously drink alcoholic drinks to hold a constant low level of intoxication going forward, including while working their job as well as their time at home. The experiment proves itself to come with upsides as well as major difficulties, as it becomes a balancing act for each of them to adjust to the new lifestyle.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F672d316a30cbb-profile%20nov%202024.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

While international movies always seem to be harder sells for more general audiences, Another Round is easily one of the most accessible and adaptable international films to be released in recent memory. The film's very simple yet highly effective premise leads to a great deal of comedy and shenanigans, which are only further amplified by the terrific performances of everyone involved and the great directing style of Thomas Veinterberg. The film made enough of a splash worldwide that there are even plans for an English remake starring Leonardo DiCaprio.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/1182231cf2d8b7b56b8bd1cf7a2bbe28.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Anya Taylor-Joy as Emma smiling at Mia Goth's character in Emma.

blocks.x: Image via Focus Features

Adapted from the iconic classic Jane Austen novel, Emma follows the story of the well-meaning but selfish young woman of Emma, living in 1800s England as she meddles with the love lives of her friends and family. As she continues to play matchmaker in the lives of everyone around her, Emma soon enough finds herself unknowingly at the center of her own romance as it begins to unfold around her.

The story of Emma has been adapted to film a multitude of times throughout film history, both through direct adaptations of the novel and loose adaptations like the teen sensation Clueless. However, Autumn de Wilde's Emma is able to perfectly combine the themes and attributes of the original novel with enough modern flair and conventions to make it an exceptional comedic period piece. The true highlight of the film is Anya Taylor-Joy, who provides an iconic and scene-stealing comedic performance in the leading role of Emma.

21
'Theater Camp' (2023)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/07/theater-camp-jimmy-tatro-ayo-edebiri-1.jpeg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Jimmy Tatro as Troy and Ayo Edebiri as Janet walking down a street in Theater Camp

blocks.x: Image Via Searchlight

A love letter to the small-scale, chaotic nature of summer camp and amateur theater, Theater Camp is equal parts defined by its endless charm as it is by its embracing of its nonsensical supporting cast. The mockumentary follows a scrappy upstate New York theater falling into shambles after its beloved founder ends up in a coma, forcing the eccentric staff and the founder's failure of a son to keep the camp afloat for the summer.

No other film has such an intelligent, fundamental understanding of the ins and outs of youth theater quite like Theater Camp, making for the perfect setup to absolutely make fun of it with pitch-perfect satire. Each member of the supporting cast gets time to shine, whether it be the charmingly idiotic Troy (Jimmy Tatro) or the inseparable pair of Amos (Ben Platt) and Rebecca-Diane (Molly Gordon). While the film was originally overlooked during its theatrical release due to releasing at the same time as Barbie and Oppenheimer, it soon found a new life and fan-favorite status on streaming.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/glen-powell-smiling-and-wearing-aviators-in-richard-linklater-s-hitman.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Glen Powell smiling and wearing Aviators at a diner in Richard Linklater's Hitman.

blocks.x: Image via Netflix

Richard Linklater has helmed a wide variety of exceptional comedy films over the years, including the likes of School of Rock and Dazed and Confused. Hit Man is simply the latest smash hit comedy from the director, using an ingenious premise to get a wide variety of laughs and mileage out of one of Hollywood's biggest rising stars, Glen Powell. The film sees Powell as Gary Johnson, a mild-mannered professor who works on the side as a fake hitman in police stings, who finds himself in the middle of a major predicament when he begins to fall for his latest client.

Hit Man fully delivers on the comedic potential of its concept, giving free rein for Powell to show off his comedic chops in a wide variety of fun and hilarious performance styles and personalities. However, what continues to make the film one of the biggest and most acclaimed comedies of the streaming service era is the signature heart and charm that is present within all of Linklater's works. The phone call sequence at the end is especially one of the greatest comedic setups in recent memory, and is emblematic of the entire film's overwhelming charm and electrifying energy.

19
'Palm Springs' (2020)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/03/another-round-2020.jpeg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Palm-Springs-(2020).jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Nyles and Sarah floating in the pool

blocks.x: Image via NEON

Palm Springs follows the story of carefree spirit Nyles and reluctant Maid of honor Sarah, who, after their brief encounter during a Palm Springs wedding, find themselves at the center of a supernatural event. The duo is stuck in an endless time loop where they are forced to repeat the day of the wedding over and over and subsequently exhaust all possibilities of what could happen on the wedding day. With endless time on their hands, the duo soon form a connection and bond, which begins to crack as the duo attempts to find a way to escape.

Time-loop movies have become a staple of comedy ever since the massively popular Groundhog Day, yet Palm Springs stands out as the first comedy since Groundhog Day to make perfect comedic use of the premise. Palm Springs understands both the inherent comedy and potential present within time loops, as well as the eventual dread and horror that come as a result of exhausted possibilities. The primary focus of the film being on a duo as opposed to a singular person only further adds to the comedic potential, as well as the inevitable crash and burn.

18
'The Drama' (2026)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/the-drama-2026.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: The Drama - 2026 - Zendaya leans her head on Robert Pattinson's shoulder

blocks.x: Image via A24

Quickly making a name for itself as one of the defining dark comedies of the decade, Kristoffer Borgli's The Drama isn't afraid to delve into some fundamentally uncomfortable subject matter while simultaneously finding the comedic elements within such unsettling concepts. The film sees happily engaged Emma (Zendaya) and Charlie (Robert Pattinson) have their bonds tested after some shocking truths from Emma's past come to life in what was supposed to be a fun game of awkward truths.

The Drama gets a lot of mileage out of pushing the strange absurdities of its painful central concept, one that can't truly be stated without spoiling the movie but undeniably is considered a major taboo to discuss in the realm of comedy. However, it's tackled with such inherent precision and finesse, focusing more on the psychological dynamics of these characters instead of the pain of the concept itself, that it allows the film to greatly succeed as one of the funniest yet darkest films of 2026.

17
'The Worst Person in the World' (2021)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/worstperson2-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Renate Reinsve as Julie running down the street in The Worst Person in the World.

blocks.x: Image via SF Studios

A strikingly prolific and brilliant coming-of-age story about the transitionary period of young adulthood, The Worst Person in the World is a singular cinematic experience that feels timeless in its execution. The film chronicles four years in the life of Julie (Renate Reinsve) as she navigates a troubled love life and struggles to find her career path. The chaos and unpredictability of her life lead her to look inward in hopes of discovering who she truly is as a person.

The Worst Person in the World provides a more intimate look at a period of time not often explored for its development and growth, yet is undeniably important and emblematic of modern human experience. The film blends its serious and impactful messaging with an array of comedic, lighthearted moments, with deeply engrossing characters to further amplify the themes and energy of the film. Even for those who don't normally watch international filmmaking, this Norwegian film is absolutely worth watching for any fans of serious dramatic rom-coms.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/the-menu-ralph-fiennes-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Chef Julian Slowik smiling softly with his crew behind him in The Menu

blocks.x: Image via Searchlight Pictures

The Menu follows the story of a couple who travel off to a coastal island in order to eat at a highly prestigious, exclusive restaurant in which the head chef, Slowik, has prepared an extensive and lavish menu. As the night progresses, it becomes more and more apparent that the planned menu and dinner are much more sinister, as the guests' lives are on the line. Already an outsider to this exclusive and high-class world, Margot attempts to do everything that she can to escape the dinner before it's too late.

The Menu is a film that is as sinister and disturbing as it is hilarious and satirical in its lambasting and portrayal of the upper class and the culture that it perpetuates. The film is filled with hilarious characters and set pieces that complement the rising tension and stakes of the film perfectly. The film is all brought together by the comedically terrifying central performance of Ralph Fiennes as Chef Slowik, who perfectly balances being a cold and calculating villainous force with the comedic service industry revenge fantasy.

items.title: Star Trek Officially Begins A New Era Today In Outposts Unknown
items.author: Chris Carter
items.summary: Star Trek is the final frontier, and it's also an endless source of creativity across multiple decades. While every iteration isn't equal in quality, Star Trek
items.text:
Star Trek is the final frontier, and it's also an endless source of creativity across multiple decades. While every iteration isn't equal in quality, Star Trek as a whole has challenged its viewers time and time again, and delivered tons of unique stories with original characters.

That's why so many people flock to specific series, or stick with just a few. If you think of the phrase "Star Trek" and close your eyes, you'll probably picture a captain, or a standout character like Worf from The Next Generation.

The characters drive the story and are often defined by who is playing the captain at any given time. For Star Trek: Outposts, the story is taking a decidedly different direction.

Star Trek: Outposts Unknown is out today on Steam, taking players to the far corners of the X'Lehari System in the 23rd century (it's "alongside" the era showcased in the Strange New Worlds TV series). Here's an overview of what you can expect:

"Lead your crew across strange new worlds in this narrative-driven outpost builder! Research, explore, and build as you face a mysterious cosmic force that threatens a new ally. Your adventure awaits, Captain! Construct complex research facilities across strange new worlds in the first-ever outpost builder set in the Star Trek universe."

In Outposts, you'll become the captain, creating a new avatar to lead this corner of the universe. While many Star Trek games let you play the captain, this one lets you run rampant in the X'Lehari System. In your own corner of the galaxy:

"Explore diverse tech and buildings trees, and carefully choose which structures will help explore and build as you face a mysterious cosmic force that threatens all life in the system. Explore the X’Lehari System with a completely original Star Trek story set in the 23rd century, alongside the era depicted in Star Trek: Strange New Worlds. Traverse through unique environments, meet new characters, and use iconic technology in your mission to render aid to a fragile civilization’s impending catastrophe."

It has a ton of potential, and if you're curious, it might be worth wishlisting to see how it lands at launch.

It's staggering, just how many Star Trek projects are coming out, even as the mainline series is taking a hiatus. Earlier this year, Star Trek: Voyager - Across the Unknown was released, a survival game where you control the well-being of the entire crew. It was released to "mostly positive" reviews on Steam, including this one:

"Played the Demo and then bought the game. Simple What if Scenario featuring the sights and sounds of USS Voyager, is it the best game ever? No. Is it fun? Yes. 30$ game featuring more or less the same gameplay loop."

There's more on the way, too. In the future, we'll also see Star Trek: Shadow Frontier, which is taking the series in a bold new direction. It's clear that Star Trek has plenty left to give, especially in the gaming arena.

items.title: So What Are We Supposed To Take Away From You Can See Everything?
items.author: Kenneth Shepard and Ash Parrish
items.summary: So, You Can See Everything, huh? A few of us here at Kotaku saw Nathan Fielder’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of Theranos, a health tech
items.text:
So, You Can See Everything, huh? A few of us here at Kotaku saw Nathan Fielder’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of Theranos, a health tech company that was shut down after Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors in 2018. The basis of the accusations was that the company’s signature device, which Theranos claimed could accurately conduct a vast assortment of blood tests on a single drop of blood, didn’t work as investors were led to believe. The film documents her final weeks with her partner and children before having to surrender herself into federal custody in Bryan, Texas.

Kenneth Shepard: And that’s only half of the Everything we See in this movie. So Ash, before we get into all there is to unpack, tell me, what was your knowledge of both Holmes and of Fielder’s work leading up to seeing this movie?

Ash Parrish: So most of my initial exposure to Nathan Fielder had been against my will. My first run-in with his work was the first season of his HBO show The Rehearsal where I felt for him both kinship and revulsion. I was fascinated and amused by the Inception-like depth to which he would pursue a subject and the results that would produce in his human guinea pigs. I’ve been hooked ever since. Less so, though, with Nathan for You which I have only seen bits and pieces of because my husband thinks it’s fucking hilarious. That show makes me want to crawl out of my flesh. Far less endearing than The Rehearsal.

As for Elizabeth Holmes, I think I saw some of the initial documentaries that had come out about her after her legal convictions but that was it. I didn’t see and didn’t care about The Dropout. But I knew her in broad strokes.

I think what lit my brain on fire with You Can See Everything is I know Fielder can get weird, and that the weirder he gets, the more human a story emerges, either from his subjects or himself (I’m thinking of the time he got a pilot’s license in the purest distillation of commitment to the bit). I wanted to see him work his eldritch neurodivergent truth powers on her to see what shakes out and HO BOY.

KS: I have avoided a lot of Fielder’s work because secondhand embarrassment makes me viscerally uncomfortable in a way that my therapist and I have had many conversations about. I watched the first episode of The Rehearsal and was like, “Oh, if it’s only going to get worse from here I have to tap out.”

For Holmes, I had only vague recollections of what happened with her and Theranos when the trailers came out because that was absolutely something outside of my orbit. I think I saw those stories coming out and kind of thought, “Ah, an American medical company being deceitful. For me, it was Tuesday.” Never watched The Dropout or really thought much about her again, to the point where when I first saw the You Can See Everything trailer I didn’t immediately recognize her. However, that trailer with Nathan and Elizabeth being inches away from each other’s face and he’s straight up asking her if she’s being deceitful sent chills down my spine.

I think anyone who has ever dealt with a narcissist or pathological liar has had a conversation like that, where they’re looking someone in the eye who, whether they truly internally believe it or not, is so committed to the “truth” they’re trying to put out that it’s almost unnerving. I was immediately brought back to a conversation I had in a coffee shop with an ex of mine in college who was very obviously lying to me, and he had to have known that I knew he was lying because I had literally laid out the facts of a situation in a way he could not feasibly debunk, and yet he dug his heels in, and I had that same expression Fielder has in the trailer of just pure annoyed disbelief, and I straight up just said “Why are you doing this?” Like, why are you committing so hard to this when the facts of the matter are laid out here. And so from this scene alone of two people where the dynamic seemed to be one person caught in dishonesty and another person just looking at them and trying to read why they’re acting like this, I felt like I had to see this movie almost as a form of catharsis for a nearly decade-old event. I don’t think I necessarily got that, and obviously after seeing it in the context of the movie, that initial scene is a bit more layered than it originally seemed. But it got me to watch something I would have probably skipped otherwise.

AP: How do you feel about Holmes now after seeing the full film? I’m honestly less concerned about her flavor of narcissistic pathology because she, for better or worse, is serving her court-mandated restitution for that. Meanwhile Billy Fucking Evans is a free man breathing free air.

KS: That is kinda the big question of the movie, right? Like, ultimately, yeah, Holmes is doing her time, I don’t frankly feel any sympathy for the people she may or may not have ripped off (motherfucking Assassin’s Creed villain Henry Kissinger was on the Theranos board?), so the fraud of it all doesn’t get me. I do think, and obviously all of this is couched as “the movie presents this in a particular way, and that is what we have to cast judgments about,” You Can See Everything does make her a sympathetic figure, and simultaneously makes a whole show of acknowledging the folly of doing so. Because I did genuinely feel for Elizabeth Holmes “the character” as she is portrayed on film. Fielder goes out of his way to show how the slightest gap in what someone says and how it is perceived can lead to a communication shit storm, and whether or not I believe that Holmes actually doesn’t understand those nuances is immaterial to how much I have seen that bullshit manifest every day as a person who works with words on the internet. A headline that people react to because of what they think it means rather than what it actually means is something we see every day in this line of work. So I think the movie showing things like the famous “Who’s on First?” comedy routine is effective in communicating this hypothetical disconnect. But then yeah, is it all an act? Is the way she and Evans basically say the exact same things to him when he’s interviewing them independently a sign that these two are ironclad con artists and Fielder maybe got too close to see it all objectively? Again, those are questions the movie asks and is at least upfront about.

I think if Holmes was being honest with Fielder during his prison visit about her knowledge of all the various insane things Evans has been doing both before and during her sentence, then who am I to tell her not to date and have children with a red-pilled Silicon Valley fuckboy when she seems happy doing so? If she didn’t know about all those things, she most certainly will now, and if she chooses to raise a family and a business with him and is truly not in any distress about it, then is this just a rich person’s version of “girl who stays with her shitty boyfriend and makes excuses for him”?

And even that kneejerk reaction feels dismissive because anyone who’s been in an abusive relationship will tell you that you will romanticize it until you can’t anymore. A man putting an AI mock-up of his partner on the internet and just shrugging at the idea of it being used for nefarious reasons? Immediate breakup. That man has no respect for you. The movie outright asks the Stockholm Syndrome question and just kinda feels like it’s hit a wall. Which, you know, ending a movie on “We don’t have a satisfactory answer to all these questions” is as valid a conclusion as any. You can see everything, but you’ll never truly know everything.

AP: Yeah I was going to ask: Do you think she’s aware enough to know she should be in distress? My alarm bells as a person with experience with narcissistic / abusive people were ringing off the whole scene with the eggs. But even then I question it because that’s a weird way for someone to whisk eggs. Does Elizabeth know that? Was that scene constructed to reinforce the narrative that she’s just too naive, too neurodivergent, and needs someone like Evans to steer her directly?

And her poor children, she had them just before she was sent away. In an interview with Fielder in WIRED, he shared that she patently did not think she was going to jail. And I can’t help but wonder if the sympathy having two little kids running around encouraged was part of a grander scheme. “You can’t send me to jail, look I have babies. Think of them.”

KS: Same. I was at the Alamo Drafthouse watching it so I wasn’t about to so much as whisper to my friends sitting next to me during the eggs scene lest their snipers take me out, but I immediately sat straight up in my chair and looked at them like “what the fuck?” And that wasn’t even remotely close to the most fucked-up thing Evans would do during the whole movie. The more charitable read that this is just their dynamic and they’re both content with it is a valid one, but from a filmmaking perspective You Can See Everything does seem to lean into the narrative that something is amiss here from the outset. They both were supposedly okay with this entire documentary project, but she is remarkably open about it, whereas he’s the one who gets cagey about answering questions or Fielder talking to her family for too long.

There’s also the added layer of, which I didn’t know going in, her father bringing up that she was raped at Stanford, which is the kind of world-shattering thing that can completely skew your relationships with other people. So again, I feel like the movie wants me to at least consider the charitable and sympathetic angle that maybe she wasn’t deceitful, but instead was someone who has been traumatized by her lived experience and now sees the world through a more neurodivergent lens. The human part of me wants to see it that way, but everything else that’s happening around it makes me hesitant to do so. Like even shit where she’s like “I never let people see me cry” and then seems to just start crying on command. Could Elizabeth Holmes be a neurodivergent woman who has dealt with a lot of trauma, is naive, got in over her head, and is also possibly a pathological liar? Does the founder of Theranos contain multitudes like Walt Whitman once said?

AP: I don’t think those two things are at odds with each other. And this is a way to help one reinforce the other. I believe, like any ND person, myself included, that effective communication is fraught. I don’t, can’t, believe that it could be SO impenetrable to her that she doesn’t grasp why people interpreted the “can” in “This machine can run all kinds of tests” as meaning what Fielder said it meant.

If that kind of miscommunication gaffe is the hill you’re choosing to die on…

And it’s made more sinister by Evans in that moment being like “See the kind of whimsical spirit she is!” in this gross paternalistic kind of way.

KS: It is the weird game Fielder has to play here that he does, to some extent, have to at the very least interrogate those claims and ideas in good faith, no matter how absurd they might sound. In which case, mission pretty well accomplished.

KS: In some ways Seyfried felt like the audience stand-in because Fielder’s not gonna be like “fuck this man, actually,” so thanks to her for her service. Buried in the vast and sooty-fingered Summer Eternal anthology, there's an interview with former BioWare developer and Dragon Age lead writer David Gaider, who is now creative director at Stray Gods outfit Summerfall Studios. The interview is a podcast-length account of BioWare's transformations over Gaider's career, stretching back to Baldur's Gate 2. Amongst other things, it explains why the Dragon Age games feel so different from sequel to sequel.

Gaider discusses the original trilogy's fortunes under RPG-phobic parent company Electronic Arts, commenting that 2009's Dragon Age: Origins made it to release partly thanks to "sunk cost" thinking after EA bought the studio. He also talks about Dragon Age's lack of a properly defined vision, early on, which led to a lot of overcorrection between releases. As regards Origins, there was something of a faction war initially between departments over what exact flavour of fantasy fiction the new RPG should draw on.

"When we started, Dragon Age's big premise was 'it's D&D, but it's not," Gaider began. "We'll just file off the serial numbers enough to make it our own. That was not great because there are different kinds of fantasy."

Specifically, a rift emerged at BioWare between developers who wanted to channel Tolkien, and those who wanted to invoke Robert E. Howard's Conan the Barbarian stories. "If you look back at the E3 Expo, where we announced the existence of Dragon Age, and you watch the video, you will see," Gaider went on (the screening in question was behind closed doors, sadly, so all I can do is point you towards IGN's coverage at the time). "It was mostly made by our art department. They were part of the Conan group. And if you watch it, you'll see sexy sorceresses, the fighter is this bare-chested barbarian riding around… it looks very Conan.

Watch on YouTube

"And that part of the team was determined that their vision was set out," he said. "The design department was mostly like, 'no, this is Lord of the Rings, man, okay? Fuck Conan.' But Art didn't want to listen to us, so we're like 'If you're going to ignore us, we'll ignore you.' And that's really why the Dragon Age that came to be is the way it is. If you look at Dragon Age: Origins, if I said to you, this is the art style of a Conan world with the writing style of a Lord of the Rings, then you'd be like, 'Oh.'"

When teams are at odds in this way, it's helpful to have a third group intervene to thrash out a compromise. The producers, for example. Unfortunately, Gaider continued, Dragon Age's production team had their own wild ideas about the project's direction - they thought it should be Diablo. This did, in fairness, have some kind of unifying effect. "Both the art department and the design department completely ignored them. Like, no, we're not doing Diablo."

Nonetheless, the producers persisted. "They wanted that if you hit creatures, they'd just explode in blood," Gaider said. "We actually had presentations where the people in charge were like, 'Yeah, Dragon Age, we want that the theme is blood! Dripping with blood!' And I'm like, 'That's not a theme.' They did get their way a little bit, Dragon Age was pretty bloody. People did almost explode in blood. We had to tone it down a bit because that just didn't feel right."

I realise there's a serious argument being made here about the necessity of knowing your game's heart, before you commit to knocking out scripts, models and trailers, but I am also having fun imagining the inter-departmental squabbles. I picture Gaider bumping into one of the Dragon Age artists outside an elevator in Edmonton, sometime in 2004. The artist's eyes narrow. "Tell me, David," they growl. "What is best in life?" Gaider's knuckles whiten. "To take the ring to Mordor, throw it into Mount Doom, and hear the lamentation of Sauron," he hisses. At this point the elevator doors open and a producer appears, apoplectic and roaring: "Ahh, fresh meat!"

According to Gaider – who would eventually become "vision keeper" or "educator" for Dragon Age as a series - BioWare did a much better job of getting the band together with Mass Effect, mostly thanks to project director Casey Hudson.

"Mass Effect went through much the same kind of struggle," he said. "It's science fiction. It's 'their Star Wars,' is what that was supposed to be. But there's so many different kinds of science fiction. And they had the benefit that Casey Hudson was the responsible person, and realised sooner than Dragon Age did that we need a singular vision. And he eventually put his foot down and said, 'This is what it is.'

"I think, honestly, Mass Effect as a series had a much stronger throughline of vision," Gaider concluded. "This is a game that is very clear on what it is and what it isn't. Whereas Dragon Age started off kind of a jumble and we figured it out as we went. With Dragon Age: Origins, versus Dragon Age II, versus Dragon Age: Inquisition, you've clearly got a team that is figuring out the world of the series by the seat of their pants and reacting with each release."

To address the Qunari in the room, here: Gaider left many years before Dragon Age: The Veilguard, whose development was a whole 'nother layer of troubled. EA - who are now owned by a consortium consisting mostly of Saudi Arabia's sovereign investment fund - appear to have paused the series in the wake of Veilguard, though modders are trying to keep the flames alive.

What's your poison, then? Conan, Tolkien or Diablo? While we're talking office politics at giant corporate developers, the Summer Eternal anthology also harbours a lengthy chat with Dragon Age's former executive producer, Mark Darrah. He has words of warning about "over-specialised" studios and $100 million projects that need to sell ridiculous quantities to break even. As far as I can remember, Darrah doesn't spend any of his chinwag lamenting the great Diablo-like that might have been if it weren't for the Gandalf-loving pinkos in the writing team or those Cromulent numpties in art.

Disk Cleanup

(Image credit: Future)Welcome to Disk Cleanup, our regular weekend feature delving into the PCs of PC gaming luminaries. Come back every weekend to read a new interview, digging into the important questions, like "How tidy is your desktop?" and "What game will you never uninstall?"

Joe Ziegler might be best known for his role guiding the design of big competitive shooters, but his formative gaming experiences were with point-and-click adventures like King's Quest. "There was something so clever about trying to use all this knowledge about random things like fairy tales to try to solve puzzles inside of the game," he says. "It was just that 'A-ha!' moment where videogames could be these really engaging ways for you to be clever and creative."

Ziegler started out at Pandemic Studios, where he worked as a mission designer on 2009's The Saboteur. But he is best known as game director on Riot's hugely popular arena shooter Valorant, and his more recent oversight of Bungie's extraction-shooter revival of Marathon, which he assumed leadership of in March 2024 following the dismissal of former director Christopher Barret.

Following Marathon's launch, Ziegler left Bungie and is currently working on a new, unrevealed project: "My goal ultimately when I'm thinking about 'What do I direct and what do I make?' is 'Where can I make the coolest thing with the coolest people?'" he explains. "That's part of the reason I went to Bungie in the first place. And now, as I'm looking at this next thing, I'm also in that headspace."

Ziegler took a break from his secret project to show me around the best loot spots of his Steam library. We talked JRPGs, ARPGs, and the forgotten Bungie game that led him to work on Marathon.

What game are you currently playing?

(Image credit: FromSoftware)I'm playing a couple right now. I'm revisiting Elden Ring Nightreign again. I play it socially with some friends. We're doing a lot of the Deep of Night and purple boss stuff. It's a game that's near and dear to me.

It's funny because my initial reaction to it was like, "What is this game?" But over the course of time, it's combined my love of soulslikes—I really like a lot of soulslikes—with this multiplayer roguelike, where every run you're building a build and trying to conquer the challenge that's in front of you. The level of difficulty keeps it constantly a mastery challenge—which is something that definitely motivates me.

It's a game that's near and dear to me.

Joe Ziegler

A lot of it is playing off of your mastery and understanding of stats that exist in Elden Ring. I played a lot of Elden Ring, so it was easier for me to onboard, and I can imagine for people who have not played a lot of Elden Ring, it's impossible to onboard into. But if you do, you begin theorycrafting a lot of things when you're on your run. You're like, "Oh, should I go for a bleed-based run this time around, am I using the right character with the right arcane stats to do that?" All of your knowledge and all of your capability … come together.

The other game I'm playing is Star Wars: Galactic Racer. Someone called it Race the Spire and I totally agree. It's basically a roguelike racer, and I don't know if it's just the change in pace of playing a racer again, but I think it's been really interesting to see that level of roguelike progression folded into a racer … where all the different components of thinking about your racer become more flexible and interesting from a buildcrafting standpoint.

What was the previous game you played, and is it still installed?

(Image credit: Bungie)Oddly enough, I was revisiting Destiny 2. A couple of people I know were getting back into Destiny 2 a little bit, so it was fun to jump in with them and experience going through some stuff.

I have about 730 hours, so I'm not as hardcore as a lot of other people. But D2 is definitely comfort food …. I was originally playing a Warlock. I played a Warlock for quite a few years, and then I just recently went back to playing a Titan, and I was levelling up my Titan again. And I was playing mostly a prismatic spec.

Way back when I was 16, I played a lot of Myth 2 [with] a friend of mine from high school. And oddly enough, it came with a box that had a ticket to go to E3 at the time, which was really crazy. So the first E3 I went to was because Bungie shipped these tickets. I talked to Jason Jones about this, and he was like, "That was all Alex Seropian, and Alex Seropian's marketing mentality was that." So that's how I remember Bungie. Of course I played Halo, just like everybody else who lived in America.

There were a lot of disagreements across the place.

Joe Ziegler

It was the legacy of all those games, Halo to Destiny, that really drove me to work at Bungie … it was actually a couple of friends that I used to work with at Pandemic who were at Bungie who approached me, and one of them was Justin Truman, the former CEO … we started working on something. But then they needed help on the Marathon project, so I went over to help advise and then they asked me to come take over direction for it, and I did that.

It's always interesting jumping into a project when it's already been started, because part of it is getting everyone together and being like, "What are we trying to do here?" And sometimes some teams will find a unanimous voice, everybody knows what they're doing, and some other teams will have very disparate ideas of what they're doing …. I found this project was… it had some areas where there were definitely some ideas about where we were going, but there were a lot of disagreements across the place.

So part of where I was advising was trying to bring those all together and be like, "Hey, what is the cohesive place you want to go to? And how do we get there?" And then when we landed on that, I could help them drive that.

I'll say this about Bungie, which I really like, and it's still very true about Bungie: it lives in two worlds. One is this world where there's a lot of legacy to live up to, which is a lot of pressure. But there's also this other side of it, which is that it's a very egoless company. In a lot of cases, they are always looking for some way to improve, and the way they do that is, oftentimes, by bringing in people who are new to help them figure out what they are missing.

What is the oldest game (by release date) currently installed on your PC?

(Image credit: Lucasfilm Games)The Secret of Monkey Island—1990 was when it was released. And that's pretty long ago, 36 years now! I feel old.

It's funny, because I've never had the luxury of talking to Ron Gilbert or Tim Schafer, or any of the guys who worked on this whole game. But I will say that The Secret of Monkey Island was formative for me in that adventure game, discovery loop way. Partly because it combined the clever puzzle solving that is iconic for point and click adventure games from that era. But I think that it's that cleverness, that irreverence, that idea of everything being both a pun and world play, and how it plays out, that resonated with me a lot.

What is the highest number of hours you have in any given game, according to Steam?

(Image credit: Grinding Gear Games)Ooh, this is going to show my other addiction. I love ARPGs. Path of Exile. I have 3,437.5 hours.

ARPGs to me are [about the] buildcrafting and the cleverness of putting things together. And I think Path of Exile is the most freeform version of that. The level of experimentation you can get in that game is so wide in terms of thinking about how you can make builds.

I play a variety of builds. I have a fondness for playing Totem builds, and then second to that is, when I'm feeling really lazy, I like one-button builds, like Whirlwind builds … that's the fun part of Path of Exile, to be honest, is that it's just such a Rube Goldberg machine of effects and things that you can make, and you're just trying to figure out how to deal the most damage and kill things the fastest.

I think I've changed my expectation around ARPGs because of Path of Exile. It's funny because I've played Path of Exile 2, and it's a little bit more limiting, and it totally makes sense because it's built around more of an action environment. But I definitely feel like Path of Exile one was more meant for me.

What game will you never, ever uninstall?

(Image credit: Disney)This is a gimme for anybody who knows me, and it's a hint that exists on every interview that I've done, because I wear a Kingdom Hearts necklace on every single one, and that's the game I'll probably never uninstall.

For all its confusing and overly complicated narrative, it's still a story about growing up.

Joe Ziegler

I have this weird tradition where, every once in a while, I'll go back and play through all those games. Part of it is nostalgia, because you're harking back to a time when you were younger and you had a summer break. And honestly, Kingdom Hearts, for all its confusing and overly complicated narrative, it's still a story about growing up, right?

They're all kind of packaged together now, but I will say my favourite is Kingdom Hearts 2. I think it's the one that's most likely to make anyone tear up. I think it has to do with the identity of Roxas and Sora, and the two different sides of that character. The soul that exists there. There's something about innocence that can be painted in different ways. That's really fascinating in terms of characterisation, how they can live two different lives, but they can be so similar to one another, and how they're so connected that way. It's really cool.

What's a piece of non-gaming software installed on your PC that you simply couldn't live without?

(Image credit: Getty Images)Any online gamer would probably say the same thing, which is Discord. I've been at companies where we've used it for work. I use it almost every night to hang out with my friends and game. We use it to post dumb stuff to each other. It's just the default social hub for my close friends.

Our little group is a few friends I've been really close with since the Riot days, and so we've changed up games a lot … I will say that every time a new World of Warcraft expansion comes out, we probably play it.

WoW is the other thing I've played a lot, but that's not a Steam game. I will say that I have over three-years of in-game time in WoW, so that's way too high. And we counted one time on Valorant, me and the technical director of Valorant had basically had a comparison like "Which of us has spent more time in Wow?" And I think he came in just around two years, and I came in around three years. I was like, "This is insane."

I would say everybody in the industry was playing WoW a lot for a long time …. I think there's a lot to be said that's positive about the gameplay, and I think a lot of people point to that. But my theory, if you want to hear it, is that it was social media before social media. It was basically the common space that a lot of people could get together and socialise while playing. It was before the Discord era, before any social media hub or even Twitch, right? Back in the Justin TV days. It was the place you could default to go into and get things done, but also just hang out with people.

How tidy is your desktop screen?

Not at all. There's two reasons for this. One is because I change up technology at least every couple of years. So trying to keep everything tidy feels like a fool's errand, because this machine I have is probably about a year old … but the other thing is that I rarely am ever on my desktop. Most of the time, it's covered with some [other] screen. It's either my browser or Discord. So I never really see my desktop. I never access anything from my desktop.

Not at all. There's two reasons for this. One is because I change up technology at least every couple of years. So trying to keep everything tidy feels like a fool's errand, because this machine I have is probably about a year old … but the other thing is that I rarely am ever on my desktop. Most of the time, it's covered with some [other] screen. It's either my browser or Discord. So I never really see my desktop. I never access anything from my desktop.
